content:
Fireflies.ai Transcript — Internal/External

Meeting: HelioBank x Redwood — priority routing / quotas / overload behavior deep dive
Date: Jan 21, 2025
Time: 11:00 AM PT
Duration: 54 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke, Mina Haddad, Amara Diallo, Lauren Bishop
HelioBank: Priya S. (Platform Eng), Dan H. (SRE), Marta K. (ML Platform), Jules R. (Security)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
- HelioBank asked for specifics on how Redwood handles overload without impacting enterprise endpoints.
- Redwood walked through tier-aware admission control (per-tenant/per-route/per-region limits), priority lanes, and standardized 429 responses.
- Discussed edge cases: retry storms, regional degradation, config propagation delays, and fail-open vs fail-closed behavior.
- Agreed on follow-ups: share error payload examples, propose initial lane reservation, and align Dedicated vs Hosted expectations.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Per-route rate limits vs quotas (daily/monthly)
2) Priority routing model and “enterprise lanes”
3) Behavior during overload (429 vs degraded model vs queueing)
4) Observability: what metrics HelioBank will see + how to alert
5) Dedicated capacity and SLA wording

Questions (auto-generated)
- If a single client misbehaves, can it take down a region for everyone?
- Do quotas apply per region or globally?
- What happens if your policy/config service is down?
- How do you avoid starving self-serve traffic entirely?

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send sample 429 payloads + Retry-After guidance.
- HelioBank to send top routes + retry policy.
- Redwood to propose enterprise lane reservation targets.

---
Transcript

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, cool. I think we’re good to go. Thanks everyone for joining. This is the technical deep dive on the priority routing and quotas and what happens when things go sideways, basically.

[00:12] Priya S.: Yep. Thanks Liam. We’ve been, uh, we’ve had a couple incidents with another provider where a single workload kind of… took out the whole inference cluster. So we want to make sure we understand how you all do protection.

[00:28] Liam O'Rourke: Totally. And Mina and Amara are here because they’re closest to routing and gateway enforcement. Lauren can speak to Dedicated and what we can commit to.

[00:39] Mina Haddad: Hey everyone.

[00:41] Amara Diallo: Hi.

[00:42] Lauren Bishop: Hey.

[00:44] Dan H.: Hi all.

[00:46] Marta K.: Hi.

[00:47] Jules R.: Hello.

[00:49] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Priya, maybe start with what you’re trying to protect. Is it a specific route, or like the whole chat completion thing?

[01:00] Priya S.: So we have… think of it as three main routes. One is an internal agent workflow, it’s chat completions with tool calling. Another is embeddings at high volume for search indexing, and then reranking. The scary one is the agent because it retries. Like it will do multiple calls per user action.

[01:20] Dan H.: And we saw a retry storm. It wasn’t even super high QPS, but it multiplied, and the provider started queueing, then timeouts, then more retries, and it just cascaded.

[01:33] Mina Haddad: That’s the exact failure mode we design for. There are two broad controls: (1) admission control at the edge — rate limits, quotas, and burst handling — and (2) priority-aware queueing in the router so enterprise traffic gets a protected lane even if the shared fleet is getting hammered.

[01:55] Priya S.: When you say lane, is it like separate clusters?

[01:59] Mina Haddad: Not necessarily separate clusters. It’s more like separate queues and a reservation policy. Requests are tagged by tier (enterprise vs self-serve) and by route key. The router admits requests into different queues, and schedulers pull from those with a priority policy that ensures enterprise doesn’t get drowned.

[02:22] Dan H.: Is it strict priority? Because that can starve everything else.

[02:26] Mina Haddad: Good question. It’s not “enterprise always wins forever.” We do priority with bounded fairness. In practice it’s like: enterprise lane has reserved capacity, but we also set bounds so that lower tiers still make progress. And we can tune this per region and per route group.

[02:48] Liam O'Rourke: And to frame it: the goal is if you’re an enterprise endpoint and something else goes crazy, you still hit your SLO — within reason — and you get clear signals when you’re at your own limits.

[03:04] Marta K.: What is the “clear signals” part? Like, do we see 429? Or do you queue and then it times out?

[03:11] Amara Diallo: We prefer to fail fast with a standardized 429 when you’ve hit a configured limit or when the system is in protective mode. The response includes a Retry-After header and a reason code. That way clients can back off rather than pile on.

[03:29] Marta K.: Okay. We need to know if Retry-After is seconds, milliseconds, and if it’s consistent across regions.

[03:36] Amara Diallo: Seconds, integer seconds. And yes consistent semantics. There’s a request id header as well so you can correlate in support tickets.

[03:47] Dan H.: What are the reason codes? Like is it “rate_limit” vs “capacity”?

[03:51] Amara Diallo: Exactly. Think: RATE_LIMIT, QUOTA_EXCEEDED, and OVER_CAPACITY. And sometimes POLICY_DENY if a route is temporarily disabled — but that’s more rare.

[04:06] Priya S.: Can you distinguish if we’re being throttled because we’re noisy versus you’re having an incident?

[04:12] Mina Haddad: We can. OVER_CAPACITY is basically: the fleet is telling us it’s saturated, or a region is degraded, and we’re shedding load to protect latency. RATE_LIMIT is deterministic per your configured per-route rate, and QUOTA is budget.

[04:30] Dan H.: How do you detect “fleet is saturated”? GPU utilization is sometimes misleading.

[04:35] Mina Haddad: Yep, GPU util lies. We primarily use queue depth and prefill/decode saturation signals from the runtime. We look at things like “how long requests are waiting” and “tokens per second headroom” rather than raw utilization.

[04:52] Lauren Bishop: And from a customer comms perspective, when we’re in OVER_CAPACITY protective mode, we want the behavior to be predictable and explainable — not just random timeouts.

[05:04] Jules R.: On security: do you log all throttling decisions? Like audit logs?

[05:09] Liam O'Rourke: For enterprise, yes, we can provide audit events for policy enforcement changes and access. For per-request throttling, we log metrics and sampled request logs. If you’re in Private/VPC we can align with your retention requirements.

[05:24] Jules R.: Okay. We care about data residency too. If one region is degraded, do you fail over to another region automatically?

[05:32] Mina Haddad: Only if you enable cross-region fallback, and only within whatever residency constraints are configured. Otherwise we degrade in-region: shed low priority, and keep enterprise lane healthy.

[05:47] Priya S.: Let’s talk about quotas vs rate limits. We have internal finance asking for monthly token caps.

[05:55] Amara Diallo: Right. Rate limits are short-window — like requests per second or tokens per second — enforced at the gateway. Quotas are longer windows (daily/monthly). Quota enforcement depends on metering, so we design it to be resilient to delayed telemetry.

[06:14] Dan H.: Delayed telemetry meaning you might undercount for a while.

[06:18] Amara Diallo: Exactly. The policy for that can be “fail open” to not break production on a telemetry glitch, and then catch up, or “fail closed” if you want hard spend caps.

[06:30] Priya S.: We probably want fail-open for production but with alerts.

[06:35] Lauren Bishop: That’s the default recommendation. We can put a hard stop on non-prod keys, or enforce stricter for specific tenants. But for your main prod tenant, fail-open + alerting tends to avoid self-inflicted outages.

[06:52] Marta K.: You said per-route keys. How do you define a route? We have multiple models but same endpoint.

[06:59] Amara Diallo: Route key is typically method + path + “logical operation.” For chat, it’s like /v1/chat/completions, but we can also segment by model family if needed, or by a “deployment id” you pass. We avoid super high-cardinality keys, but for enterprise we can get fairly specific.

[07:22] Dan H.: We actually want segmentation because embeddings should not steal capacity from chat.

[07:27] Mina Haddad: That’s a common setup: separate policies per route group, and then separate lane allocations. You can think of it as: chat enterprise lane reservation is protected; embeddings can be throttled earlier.

[07:40] Priya S.: But is it token-based or request-based? Embeddings requests can be big.

[07:46] Amara Diallo: Both exist. Request-rate limiting is easiest; token-based is more accurate. For chat we often do tokens/sec shaping when customers have spiky prompts. There are some estimation errors at the gateway because you don’t know output tokens ahead of time, but we handle with conservative estimates and then runtime feedback.

[08:10] Marta K.: So you might throttle us based on predicted tokens? That’s tricky.

[08:14] Mina Haddad: We try to not be surprising. For chat, we can enforce on input tokens at the edge, and then enforce output token throughput in the router/runtime with backpressure. The 429 will still say the reason.

[08:30] Dan H.: Do you ever do 503 instead of 429?

[08:33] Amara Diallo: Rarely. 503 would indicate a platform fault rather than customer limits. For overload protection, we prefer 429 with Retry-After.

[08:44] Liam O'Rourke: And your client libraries should treat 429 differently than 5xx. We’ll send guidance.

[08:52] Priya S.: One thing: we use exponential backoff but we have multiple services. If they all back off the same, you can get thundering herd.

[09:01] Dan H.: Yeah, plus our timeout is 12 seconds and max retries 3.

[09:06] Mina Haddad: Yeah, jitter is key. Also, honoring Retry-After rather than guessing. We can suggest a pattern: immediate retry only for idempotent calls and only once, then backoff with full jitter, max cap.

[09:23] Marta K.: What about streaming? If we stream tokens, can you cut it off midstream during overload?

[09:29] Mina Haddad: We avoid terminating active streams unless absolutely necessary. Admission control is primarily before the request starts. If the runtime enters extreme saturation, we might reduce concurrency for new requests rather than kill ongoing ones.

[09:46] Dan H.: Okay. Another question: What happens if your config service is down? Like the policy engine can’t be fetched.

[09:53] Amara Diallo: Gateway caches policy config. If it can’t refresh, it uses last-known-good for a TTL. After that, it can either fail-open (let traffic through) or fail-closed (throttle). For enterprise, we typically do last-known-good + conservative defaults if stale, not a hard stop.

[10:16] Priya S.: Conservative defaults meaning lower limits?

[10:18] Amara Diallo: Not necessarily lower. More like: keep your committed enterprise lane behavior stable, and avoid enabling aggressive new protections if config is uncertain. We can walk through the exact fallback logic in a doc.

[10:35] Lauren Bishop: And that’s also why rollouts are staged. We don’t flip everything globally at once.

[10:42] Jules R.: Can we get notified if you’re operating on cached policy? That’s an operational risk.

[10:47] Mina Haddad: Yes, we have metrics for config freshness and propagation lag. We can also expose status in Console for enterprise.

[10:58] Dan H.: That would be good. We got burned by propagation delays elsewhere.

[11:03] Liam O'Rourke: Noted. We’ll include that in the follow-up.

[11:08] Priya S.: Let’s talk about Dedicated. We’re debating Hosted vs Dedicated. Our concern: if we’re on Hosted, do we still get protected lane?

[11:18] Lauren Bishop: Hosted enterprise gets priority lanes, but Dedicated is stronger isolation because you have reserved GPU pools. That said, even Dedicated can overload itself if one route goes wild. So you still need per-route protections inside your Dedicated deployment.

[11:39] Priya S.: So Dedicated isn’t a magic bullet.

[11:41] Lauren Bishop: Right. It prevents “someone else’s traffic” from impacting you, but it doesn’t prevent “you impacting you.” That’s where quotas/rate limits/priority lanes per route help.

[11:54] Dan H.: If we buy Dedicated with, say, X tokens/sec, do you guarantee that per route or overall?

[12:01] Lauren Bishop: Overall throughput for the deployment, with guidance for per-route shaping. We can discuss an addendum for specific hot routes, but it’s usually framed as SLO + capacity reservation rather than a strict per-route TPS guarantee.

[12:18] Marta K.: We would like explicit behavior during partial failure. Like if a GPU node dies, what happens.

[12:25] Mina Haddad: The protection model is the same: enterprise lane has reserved share, so as capacity drops, low priority traffic is shed first. The router can also divert to compatible model variants if you allow fallback — for example a slightly smaller model — but that’s opt-in.

[12:46] Priya S.: We probably don’t want model fallback without us knowing.

[12:49] Liam O'Rourke: That’s common. You can disable fallback, and then it’s purely queue/shedding behavior.

[12:58] Dan H.: On the shedding: is it per-tenant or global? Because we don’t want our batch embeddings to be dropped if it’s quiet, but we also don’t want it to compete with chat.

[13:10] Mina Haddad: It’s both. You can set per-tenant limits, and also per-route. We can set embeddings to have a lower priority lane, or even “background” lane, so chat is always protected.

[13:23] Amara Diallo: And gateway enforcement helps too: embeddings can have stricter burst limits.

[13:30] Priya S.: When you say “burst,” do you allow burst above the steady rate?

[13:34] Amara Diallo: Yes, token bucket style. You have a sustained rate and a burst capacity. That’s important for workloads that spike but then idle.

[13:48] Marta K.: Can we tune burst by time of day? Like we batch index at night.

[13:53] Amara Diallo: We can do scheduled policy changes, or you can have separate API keys/tenants for batch vs prod. Scheduled policies are possible but we’d want to ensure you don’t create a footgun.

[14:10] Dan H.: What about multi-region. If we’re active-active in us-east and eu-west, do limits share state?

[14:17] Amara Diallo: Rate limits are enforced per region at the gateway. Quotas can be global (aggregated) but with delayed metering. For strict global enforcement in real time, that’s hard without a centralized counter; we typically recommend per-region limits plus a global quota with some slack.

[14:39] Jules R.: For residency, EU traffic must stay EU.

[14:42] Mina Haddad: Understood. Then you’d run separate regional policies and no fallback across the boundary.

[14:52] Liam O'Rourke: Can I ask what providers you’re evaluating? Just for context.

[14:56] Priya S.: We have some workloads on Bedrock, we’ve tried OpenAI for prototypes, and we looked at Together for open models. But we need more control over behavior under load.

[15:09] Liam O'Rourke: Makes sense.

[15:11] Dan H.: Specifically, the “everyone gets slow” scenario. We’d rather have a subset get 429 quickly.

[15:18] Mina Haddad: Same philosophy here: keep tail latency under control by shedding early and predictably.

[15:28] Marta K.: How do you decide when to shed? Like what threshold.

[15:33] Mina Haddad: We use backpressure signals. For example: if queue depth exceeds a threshold for N seconds, or if prefill saturation crosses a line. There’s some hysteresis to avoid flapping.

[15:48] Dan H.: Is that per model? Because models have different token rates.

[15:52] Mina Haddad: It’s per “backend pool” which maps to model + hardware class. So yes, effectively per model deployment.

[16:02] Priya S.: Okay. Can we see these signals?

[16:05] Mina Haddad: You’ll see aggregated metrics: throttled rate by reason, lane utilization, queue depth percentiles. You won’t see raw internal GPU counters, but you’ll see enough to understand what’s happening.

[16:20] Dan H.: We need to page on it. Like if our enterprise lane is close to saturated.

[16:26] Mina Haddad: Exactly. We can set alerts on lane utilization and on 429 spikes, but we’ll tune to avoid paging during planned load tests.

[16:37] Liam O'Rourke: We can also integrate with your on-call via webhooks, but let’s keep that for later.

[16:45] Priya S.: One more on fairness. You said bounded fairness. Can you quantify.

[16:51] Mina Haddad: In plain terms: enterprise has reserved share, say 60% of capacity. If enterprise is using less than that, the rest is available to other tiers. If enterprise is using more, it can borrow beyond 60% up to a cap, but we still guarantee a minimum service rate for lower tiers so they’re not completely starved. The exact numbers are tunable.

[17:16] Dan H.: So it’s kind of like weighted fair queuing.

[17:19] Mina Haddad: Similar outcome, yes. The internal implementation is optimized for our routing stack, but conceptually it’s weighted with guardrails.

[17:30] Marta K.: And per-route? Like two enterprise routes.

[17:33] Mina Haddad: Within enterprise, we can also segment. Some customers have “hot route A” and “hot route B” with different weights.

[17:43] Priya S.: That’s what we want. The agent route should win over embeddings even if both are ours.

[17:50] Mina Haddad: Yep.

[17:52] Amara Diallo: At the gateway side, we can also enforce separate per-route rate limits, so embeddings can’t create a backlog.

[18:02] Dan H.: If we do everything right, can we avoid timeouts entirely?

[18:07] Mina Haddad: You can reduce them significantly. But if your client timeout is too low and you have long generation lengths, you’ll still time out. The protections help prevent systemic tail latency blowups.

[18:23] Marta K.: Our max output tokens is 2k sometimes.

[18:27] Mina Haddad: That’s fairly large. You’ll want streaming and maybe a per-request max. Also, long outputs are more sensitive to decode saturation.

[18:38] Priya S.: Are there any gotchas with tool calling? Because we chain calls.

[18:43] Amara Diallo: Tool calling increases request count and can amplify retries. We recommend a client-side budget: max total attempts per user action. If you get 429, honor Retry-After and maybe degrade functionality.

[18:59] Dan H.: Degrade meaning what, show a “try again” banner.

[19:03] Liam O'Rourke: Exactly. Graceful degradation is part of the story.

[19:07] Jules R.: For compliance, do you provide an SLA that defines throttle behavior?

[19:12] Lauren Bishop: We can define SLOs and expected responses. Usually we don’t “SLA that you will never get 429” because 429 is also a customer-limit mechanism. But we can include: when at/over limit, responses are 429 with Retry-After; during platform overload, we prioritize enterprise endpoints to maintain X availability and Y latency targets.

[19:35] Priya S.: That’s exactly what we need to communicate internally.

[19:39] Dan H.: And we need to know what we’re supposed to do when we see OVER_CAPACITY. Like do we retry after the window or fail.

[19:46] Amara Diallo: We’ll provide a matrix: reason code -> recommended client action. OVER_CAPACITY: backoff with jitter, honor Retry-After; RATE_LIMIT: reduce concurrency; QUOTA: stop or use a different key/raise quota.

[20:05] Marta K.: Does Retry-After differ by reason?

[20:08] Amara Diallo: Yes. Rate limit might be small (like 1–5 seconds). Over capacity could be larger depending on queue depth.

[20:18] Priya S.: Are you calculating it dynamically?

[20:21] Amara Diallo: Yes, within bounds.

[20:25] Dan H.: Okay. Can we get a way to ask “what are my limits” via API?

[20:30] Liam O'Rourke: We have Console visibility, and there’s a roadmap for a limits endpoint. For now we can provide limits in Console and docs, and we can send you a config excerpt.

[20:46] Mina Haddad: Also, we can publish “effective limits” per route so you’re not guessing.

[20:53] Priya S.: Good.

[20:55] (crosstalk)

[20:56] Dan H.: I want to bring up an incident scenario. Say eu-west loses 30% capacity, and we have a spike at the same time. Do you automatically reduce self-serve, or does enterprise get impacted too.

[21:10] Mina Haddad: Enterprise gets impacted last. The reservation means as total capacity drops, the router uses that remaining capacity preferentially for enterprise. If enterprise demand exceeds remaining capacity, you will still see 429, but you should not see indefinite queueing.

[21:28] Dan H.: That’s the key. We want fast failure.

[21:31] Mina Haddad: Yep.

[21:33] Priya S.: What about “runaway client” inside our own tenant. Can it take out our own enterprise lane.

[21:40] Amara Diallo: If it’s the same tenant and same tier, it can, unless you segment by route or by API key. We recommend separate keys for batch jobs vs interactive, and separate route policies.

[21:55] Marta K.: We can do separate keys.

[21:58] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll note that as an implementation best practice.

[22:02] Jules R.: Does separating keys complicate audit and billing.

[22:06] Lauren Bishop: It can, but we can roll up billing by org. From audit perspective, it’s actually better — you can attribute behavior.

[22:18] Dan H.: Another thing: Do you support circuit breaker on your side? Like automatically block a client that is causing damage.

[22:26] Amara Diallo: We have “policy deny” and “temporary blocks” but we treat that carefully. More common is “adaptive throttling” where the system applies stricter limits when it detects abusive patterns.

[22:43] Mina Haddad: And SRE can toggle protections in incidents — but we try to codify it so it’s not a manual process.

[22:54] Priya S.: Okay. Can you share the exact payload of the 429? We need to update our client.

[23:01] Amara Diallo: Yep. I’ll send an example. It’ll include fields like: error.type, error.code, message, request_id, and policy details.

[23:13] Marta K.: Please include a stable code, not a message string.

[23:16] Amara Diallo: Yes, stable code.

[23:19] Dan H.: Does it include “limit” and “remaining” counts? Like typical rate limit headers.

[23:24] Amara Diallo: For some endpoints, yes: X-RateLimit-Limit, Remaining, Reset. For token-based it’s a bit trickier. But we can provide reset timestamps where possible.

[23:39] Priya S.: You said earlier you avoid high-cardinality metrics. If we have per-route and per-tenant, isn’t that high cardinality.

[23:47] Mina Haddad: We’re careful. For metrics, we aggregate by a normalized route ID and tier. Tenant labeling is restricted to enterprise tenants only, and even then, sometimes sampled. For your own Console view, you can filter to your tenant; internally we keep it bounded.

[24:07] Dan H.: So we can still see our own per-route data.

[24:10] Mina Haddad: Yes.

[24:12] Liam O'Rourke: Switching gears — do you have specific latency targets for the agent route.

[24:19] Priya S.: p95 under 1.8 seconds for short prompts, p99 under 3 seconds. But for long prompts, we accept more.

[24:30] Dan H.: Availability target 99.9 for that route.

[24:34] Lauren Bishop: Good. That gives us a basis for what lane reservation we propose.

[24:41] Marta K.: Our peaks are… I’ll send actual numbers, but roughly 120 requests/sec for the agent route in us-east at peak, and embeddings can go higher in batch.

[24:54] Mina Haddad: Great, please send the distribution too if you can — like prompt lengths and max tokens. That affects capacity planning.

[25:04] Priya S.: We can.

[25:06] Dan H.: Can you talk about how this interacts with your SDK? We use our own wrapper.

[25:12] Amara Diallo: The SDK surfaces the error code and the Retry-After header. If you use your own wrapper, just make sure you propagate those and treat 429 differently.

[25:24] Dan H.: Okay.

[25:26] Jules R.: Is there any scenario where you silently drop requests.

[25:30] Mina Haddad: No silent drops. If not accepted, you get an explicit response.

[25:35] Jules R.: Good.

[25:37] Priya S.: What about queueing. Do you ever accept and then later return 429.

[25:43] Mina Haddad: Generally no. Admission is up front. If we accept, we intend to serve. There are edge cases if the backend crashes mid-flight, but that’s a 5xx.

[25:57] Dan H.: And in that case, we retry.

[26:00] Mina Haddad: Yes, but with care.

[26:03] Liam O'Rourke: I want to be respectful of time. Let’s make sure we capture next steps.

[26:08] Priya S.: Before that, one last question: if we go Dedicated, do we still get the same 429 semantics.

[26:15] Amara Diallo: Yes. Same API surface and same error schema. That’s intentional.

[26:21] Lauren Bishop: And the Dedicated control plane can still apply per-route policies. So your app behavior doesn’t need to change.

[26:31] Dan H.: Great.

[26:33] (brief pause)

[26:34] Liam O'Rourke: Okay. Recap: Amara will send the 429 payload + headers, including Retry-After and reason codes, by Thursday. Mina will propose an initial enterprise lane reservation approach based on your peak numbers once you send them. Lauren will confirm what we can put into an SLA language around this, especially Dedicated.

[26:56] Priya S.: And we’ll send top routes plus retry policy details.

[27:00] Dan H.: Yep, including our timeouts and max retries.

[27:03] Jules R.: And I’ll follow up on region residency constraints and whether we need separate quotas per region.

[27:10] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. And I’ll schedule a follow-up in, say, early next week for 30 minutes.

[27:17] Priya S.: Works.

[27:19] Marta K.: Works.

[27:21] Liam O'Rourke: Awesome. Thanks all.

[27:25] (Meeting ends — remaining time is buffer; recording stopped)

---
Notes
- Some portions contained crosstalk; speaker attribution may be imperfect.
- Follow-up email requested: include sample 429 response and recommended client retry/backoff guidance.
